meta.title: Who really said "Don’t Like to Write, But Like Having Written"? | Quotle.info
meta.description: Not Dorothy Parker. The exact wording is Frank Norris’s, in a letter published in The Bellman in December 1915 — decades before Parker was ever credited.
meta.ogTitle: Who really said 'Don't Like to Write, But Like Having Written'?
meta.ogDescription: Frank Norris, in a letter printed in The Bellman, 4 December 1915. Parker was not credited until 1972, five years after she died.

answer.label: Not Dorothy Parker — Frank Norris, in a letter published in 1915
answer.sourceLine: This exact wording comes from a letter by the novelist Frank Norris describing his working habits, published in the Minneapolis journal The Bellman on 4 December 1915 — after his death — and reprinted widely in newspapers over the following months. Quote Investigator, whose earliest citation this is, provisionally credits Norris. The earliest link to Dorothy Parker that QI located dates from 1972, five years after she died.

source.heading: The source

docMeta.dd: 4 December 1915, volume 19, start page 642, quote page 643
Detroit Saturday Night; reprinted in newspapers through 1915–1916

source.excerpt: I write with great difficulty, but have managed somehow to accomplish 40 short stories (all published in fugitive fashion) and five novels within the last three years, and a lot of special unsigned articles. Believe my forte is the novel. Don’t like to write, but like having written. Hate the effort of driving pen from line to line, work only three hours a day, but work every day.
trail: Quote Investigator’s earliest citation is The Bellman of 4 December 1915, volume 19, quote page 643, in a piece titled ‘The Writing Grind’ that acknowledges Detroit Saturday Night. The wording matches this quote exactly the 1915 citation ↗.

The letter was Norris’s, published after his death and then syndicated: QI lists reprints in The Racine Journal News (December 1915), The Charleroi Mail (January 1916) and the Chicago Tribune (February 1916) the reprint chain ↗.

The saying then circulates for decades with no fixed owner — ascribed to an unnamed magazine writer (1936), an anonymous professional (1946), ‘Stevenson’ (1954), and used in the first person by Cornelia Otis Skinner (1964) and the critic Clive Barnes (1968) the chronological citations ↗.

The earliest attribution to Dorothy Parker that QI located is from 1972 — an episode of the sitcom The Odd Couple, in which Oscar Madison says ‘Dorothy Parker said it best for all writers’. Parker died in 1967 the 1972 citation ↗.
source.cutTag: Frank Norris, letter, in The Bellman, 4 December 1915
source.excerptNote: The quoted sentence is the third in the passage, and it is telegraphic because the whole letter is — Norris drops his subject pronouns throughout. That clipped register is why the line reads as an epigram, and why it detached so cleanly from the paragraph around it.

source.rightsNote: Free to reuse. The sentence was published in The Bellman on 4 December 1915 and reprinted in American newspapers through 1916 — all well before 1931, so the wording is in the public domain in the United States and you may reproduce the passage in full. Norris himself died in 1902. The later restatements by living writers are their own wording and a separate question. This is not legal advice.

author.name: Frank Norris
author.heading: About Frank Norris
author.metaLine: 1870–1902 · American novelist and journalist of the naturalist school
author.bio: Frank Norris wrote McTeague and The Octopus and died at thirty-two, having produced an enormous amount of work in a very short career. The letter this line comes from is a plain account of how he managed it — forty short stories and five novels in three years, three hours of writing a day, every day — which is what makes the complaint credible rather than decorative.

misattribution.heading: A line with a long queue of claimants
misattribution.intro: Almost every writer who has ever been asked whether they enjoy writing has produced some version of this, which is exactly why it has no stable owner. The Parker credit is one of the later ones, and it starts after she was dead.

items.why: The earliest Parker attribution Quote Investigator located is a 1972 episode of The Odd Couple; a 1978 Los Angeles Times interview with Larry Gelbart repeats it. Parker died in 1967, and the wording is documented from 1915 the Parker citations ↗.
A Washington Post columnist credited ‘Stevenson’ in 1954, apparently meaning Robert Louis Stevenson, who died in 1894. QI found no earlier support for the ascription the 1954 column ↗.
An Idaho paper in November 1976 wrote that ‘most writers, as Gloria Steinem has said, don’t like writing; they like having written’ — sixty-one years after the Norris letter the 1976 citation ↗.
Martin employed the line in a 2011 interview and, asked about it again in 2013, answered: ‘Which is not original again with me either. A lot of writers have said that.’ the 2013 interview ↗.

misattribution.truthLine: The exact wording belongs to Frank Norris, in a letter published in The Bellman on 4 December 1915 — fifty-seven years before anyone credited Dorothy Parker the evidence ↗.

context.heading: Why every writer claims it
lead: The line survives because it is true and slightly shameful, and because it converts a private misery into a joke you can make at a dinner party. Any working writer can say it with conviction, which means any working writer can plausibly be credited with it.

That is the mechanism behind most orphaned aphorisms. A sentiment everyone shares generates the same sentence again and again, and each new speaker is a fresh candidate for authorship — until the version with the most famous name attached crowds the rest out.
detailsBody: Quote Investigator lists at least nine claimants across a century, and the shape of the drift is consistent: the wording gets warmer as it travels. Norris’s clipped ‘don’t like…like having written’ becomes ‘I hate writing, but I love having written’ — QI notes that strengthening ‘like’ to ‘love’ is the common modification.

It is worth noting what this page is not saying. Parker may well have said something in this vein; she was asked about writing often enough. What the record does not support is the claim that she originated it, and the wording quoted here is documented in print more than fifty years before her name was attached to it.
